883.title: Tanakh
883.hook: Torah, Prophets and Writings, twenty-four books in the Jewish count
883.howItsDone: In synagogue the Torah is read from a handwritten scroll, portion by portion, in order, a passage from the Prophets called the haftarah is read with it, and some of the Writings, such as Esther on Purim, are read on particular days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last word of the Hebrew Bible: ve-ya'al, and let him go up. Your line was the call to keep climbing. Today, a step back to look at the whole shelf.

One word on the spine of a Jewish Bible: Tanakh. It isn't the name of a person or a place. It's a table of contents squeezed into one word. All along this path we've walked through it: creation and the patriarchs, Moses and the wilderness, judges and kings, prophets, poems, Job's arguments, Esther's banquet, Daniel in Babylon, Ezra and Nehemiah rebuilding. Yesterday we turned the last page. So today, what the whole thing is called, and how it's put together.
screen: `ONE WORD ON THE SPINE.` → `A TABLE OF CONTENTS IN A WORD.` → `THE LAST PAGE IS TURNED.`

segments.voice: Tanakh is built from the first letters of its three parts: T, N, K. T is for Torah, teaching: the books of Moses, Genesis to Deuteronomy, the scroll that sits in the ark in a synagogue and is read aloud, portion by portion. N is for Nevi'im, Prophets: the stories of Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, then the books of the prophets themselves, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the shorter prophets, which tradition counts together as one book called the Twelve. K is for Ketuvim, Writings: Psalms, Proverbs and Job, the scrolls like Ruth, Esther and Ecclesiastes, then Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah, and Chronicles at the close. Count Samuel, Kings, the Twelve, Ezra and Nehemiah, and Chronicles each as one, and you reach the number Jewish tradition gives: twenty-four books. The Talmud also records an order for the Prophets and the Writings. So hear Tanakh as a library with three rooms. The first is the teaching itself. The second is what happened when a people tried to live it, and the prophets who called them back. The third is everything else a people needs: songs, wisdom, love poetry, grief, history, and hard questions. And the rooms are used differently. The Torah is read from the scroll in order, week by week. Passages from the Prophets are read alongside it. Some of the Writings come out on particular days, like Esther on Purim.
screen: `T, N, K: THREE INITIALS.` · then, large: `TORAH, NEVI'IM, KETUVIM.` · `COUNTED AS TWENTY-FOUR BOOKS.` · then: `THREE ROOMS, USED DIFFERENTLY.`

segments.voice: Breathe in slowly, and on each out-breath say one name silently: Torah, teaching; Nevi'im, Prophets; Ketuvim, Writings. Go around again, and let one story you remember from this path come to mind with each room. If you pray, give thanks in words from your tradition for something you learned from them.
Tanakh. The Hebrew Bible's own name, built from its three parts: Torah, Nevi'im and Ketuvim, teaching, Prophets and Writings. Today's word.
Your line: three parts, one library. One short word holds the whole shelf. Day eight hundred eighty-three, done.

884.title: Argued into the canon
884.hook: the Mishnah records debates over whether Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes belonged (Yadayim 3:5)
884.carry: a doubt didn't throw a book out
884.howItsDone: Jewish study keeps disagreements on the page: the Mishnah and the Talmud record minority opinions by name alongside the rulings, and students learn the arguments as well as the outcomes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tanakh: Torah, Nevi'im, Ketuvim. Your line was three parts, one library. Today, who decided what went on the shelves, and did everyone agree?

The minutes of the meeting were kept. That's the surprising thing. A library of holy books could have been handed down as if it had always been settled. Instead, the rabbis of the Mishnah and the Talmud wrote down the arguments. Which books are holy? Does this one belong? What do we do with a book that seems to contradict itself? And they kept the names of the people who doubted. Earlier on this path, we heard Rabbi Akiva call the Song of Songs the holy of holies. Today, the other half of that page: the argument he was answering.
screen: `THE MINUTES WERE KEPT.` → `WHICH BOOKS ARE HOLY?` → `THE DOUBTERS ARE NAMED.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah, in tractate Yadayim, uses a strange phrase for scripture: a holy book is one that makes the hands unclean. Then it records a disagreement, almost like a transcript. One rabbi says the Song of Songs makes the hands unclean, but about Ecclesiastes there's a dispute. Another says the reverse. A third ties the question to the old schools of Shammai and Hillel. Another reports a ruling that both books do. Only then comes Akiva's strong answer: no one in Israel, he insists, ever disputed the Song of Songs; if there was a dispute, it was over Ecclesiastes. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, adds that the sages wanted to store Ecclesiastes away, because its words seemed to contradict each other, one verse praising what another seems to dismiss. Why didn't they? Because its beginning is words of Torah and its end is words of Torah. And the book does end that way, in the King James words: "Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man." So the hard middle was kept because of its frame. These books weren't slipped into the canon quietly. They were argued into it, out loud, and the record of the argument became part of the tradition too. In this record, a doubt didn't throw a book out; it made the sages look at its first and last lines.
screen: `BOOKS THAT MAKE THE HANDS UNCLEAN.` · `A DISPUTE OVER TWO BOOKS.` · then, large: `ITS BEGINNING AND END ARE TORAH.` · then: `ARGUED IN, OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Choose the Song of Songs or Ecclesiastes and hold one line from it, or this one, in the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Ask what would make someone doubt it belongs, then what would make someone fight to keep it. If you pray, give thanks in words from your tradition for the books that were kept.

885.title: Four levels of reading
885.hook: the plain meaning, the hint, the teaching and the secret: pardes
885.howItsDone: Jewish Bibles are studied with commentaries printed around the text, such as Rashi, which give the plain meaning and rabbinic teachings side by side, and students learn to say which kind of reading they are offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes were argued into the canon. Your line was a doubt didn't throw a book out. Today: now that the books are on the shelf, how do you read them?

An orchard. In the Song of Songs, the lover says, in the King James words, "Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits." The Hebrew word for orchard there is pardes. Much later, Jewish readers turned that same word into a map for reading scripture. Its four consonants, P, R, D, S, became the first letters of four ways into a text. You can walk in at the gate and see the trees, or go deeper and find what's growing underneath. Today we take the walk, and learn which gate comes first.
screen: `AN ORCHARD OF POMEGRANATES.` → `PARDES: P, R, D, S.` → `FOUR WAYS INTO A TEXT.`

segments.voice: Here are the four. P is peshat: the plain meaning, what the words say in their own setting. R is remez: the hint, pointed to by a detail, a number, a strange word choice. D is derash: the teaching drawn out by searching the text, the way the rabbis of the midrash read it, finding lessons and stories in its gaps. And S is sod: the secret, the hidden meaning the mystics looked for. Take the Song of Songs. Its peshat is a love poem between two people. Its derash, in rabbinic tradition, is the love between God and the people of Israel. Both readings live side by side. But there's an order. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, records a short rule: a verse does not depart from its plain meaning. You can read deeper, but you can't read past the words as if they weren't there. The commentator Rashi, in his note on Genesis 3:8, says he has come only for the plain sense of the verse, and for the midrash that helps settle its words. The same rule works far from any scroll: a message or a friend's sentence can be read for hidden meanings before anyone has read what it actually says. Before you hunt for the hint, the teaching or the secret, ask the plain question first: what do these words say?
screen: `PESHAT, REMEZ, DERASH, SOD.` · `ONE SONG, TWO READINGS.` · then, large: `A VERSE KEEPS ITS PLAIN MEANING.` · then: `ENTER THROUGH THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Take the last words of the Hebrew Bible, ve-ya'al, and let him go up, and stay first with the plain meaning: Cyrus, king of Persia, tells the exiles they may go up to Jerusalem and rebuild. Only then let a second reading come, what going up might mean in your own life, and keep the two side by side without letting the second erase the first. If you pray, ask in words from your tradition for clear eyes when you read.
Peshat. The plain meaning of a verse, the first of the four ways into the orchard: peshat, remez, derash, sod. Today's word.
Your line: plain meaning first. The orchard has deep roots, but you enter through the gate. Day eight hundred eighty-five.

886.title: Every word has a tune
886.hook: the Tanakh is chanted with ancient musical notes
886.carry: where the verse breathes is where its thought divides
886.howItsDone: In synagogue, a reader chants the Torah and haftarah portions from the text using the te'amim, and young people preparing for a bar or bat mitzvah learn the trope to chant their portion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the orchard of four readings: peshat, remez, derash, sod. Your line was plain meaning first. Today, our last day in the Writings, and a way of reading with your ears.

Tiny marks, above and below the letters. Open a printed Hebrew Bible and look closely: besides the letters and the vowel dots, there's a third layer of small signs. A little wedge here, a curl there, a dot beside a line. Those marks are the trope, in Hebrew te'amim, and they tell a reader how to chant. The Torah scroll itself has no vowels and no marks at all, so the reader learns them beforehand. In the synagogue the Torah is chanted, each word carrying its own short phrase of melody, and the marks say which phrase. This whole library carries its music on the page.
screen: `A THIRD LAYER OF MARKS.` → `TROPE: TE'AMIM.` → `THE TEXT IS SUNG.`

segments.voice: The trope does two jobs at once. The first is music: each mark is a little melody, and a verse becomes a chain of them. The second is sense. The same marks work like punctuation: some say pause here, strongly; some say keep going, these words belong together. So the tune is also a guide to meaning: where the verse breathes is where its thought divides. Take the first verse of the Torah, in the King James words: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." In the Hebrew, the main pause mark falls after God created, and the chant rests there, before the heaven and the earth. The Hebrew word ta'am, the singular of te'amim, can mean taste, and also sense or reason. And here's a link back to the water gate. When Nehemiah says the Levites read distinctly, gave the sense, and caused the people to understand the reading, the Talmud reads part of that verse as the te'amim themselves. On that reading, understanding a text and hearing where it divides go together. Tradition also has more than one melody for the same marks, and some books, like Esther on Purim and Lamentations on the ninth of Av, have tunes of their own. Lately we've walked through the Writings: wisdom, song, lament, Esther, Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah, Chronicles. Today, the marks that carry all of it as song.
screen: `MARKS THAT ARE MUSIC.` · `MARKS THAT ARE PUNCTUATION.` · then, large: `WHERE IT BREATHES, IT DIVIDES.` · then: `SAME MARKS, MANY MELODIES.`

If you haven't, say the first verse of Genesis slowly, pausing after God created, then going on, the heaven and the earth, and let your voice rise and fall a little, any way that feels natural.
Trope. The small marks in the Hebrew text that give each word its melody and show where the verse pauses: in Hebrew, te'amim. Today's word.
Your line: where the verse breathes is where its thought divides. The tune is also a map. That's day eight hundred eighty-six.

887.title: After the last page
887.hook: the Tanakh closes, and Jewish history goes on
887.carry: the pages ran out; the handing-on didn't
887.howItsDone: Jews read and study the Tanakh alongside the teachings of the rabbis who came after it, and some communities study Pirkei Avot, which opens with the chain of tradition from Moses, on Sabbath afternoons in the weeks after Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trope: the small marks that tell a reader how to chant. Your line was where the verse breathes is where its thought divides. Today, what comes after the last page.

Close a Tanakh and look at the last printed page. A few days ago we heard its final words: Cyrus's call to the exiles, let him go up. Then white space. And yet the people in that book did not stop on that page. Somebody went up. Somebody rebuilt a wall, planted a vineyard, argued with a neighbor, married, buried a parent, taught a child to read the very scroll that had just run out of pages. A book can end. A people keeps waking up the next morning. Today we step off the last page into the long stretch of Jewish life the Bible itself never narrates.
screen: `THE LAST PRINTED PAGE.` → `THEN WHITE SPACE.` → `A PEOPLE WAKES UP THE NEXT DAY.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, lays out an order: the Prophets close with the Twelve, the short books like Malachi, and the Writings close with Chronicles. So the Tanakh has more than one ending, and each one leans forward. Malachi's last lines tell the people to remember the teaching of Moses, then make a promise. In the King James words: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD." The Prophets end with someone still on the way. At Passover, some families pour a cup for Elijah and open the door. Then a harder turn. The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, says that when the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, died, the holy spirit of prophecy departed from Israel. But the same passage adds that people still heard a bat kol, an echo of a heavenly voice. Quieter, but not silence. So who carries the story now? The opening of Pirkei Avot answers with a chain. Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly. They gave three pieces of advice: be careful in judgment, raise up many students, and build a fence around the Torah. When the prophets go quiet, the answer is students.
screen: `MORE THAN ONE ENDING.` · then, large: `I WILL SEND YOU ELIJAH THE PROPHET.` · `PROPHECY GOES QUIET.` · `A CHAIN OF HANDS: RAISE UP STUDENTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ending in your own life, a graduation, a move, a funeral, a last day at a job, something that looked like the last page. Now look at the first ordinary morning after: who handed you something, or whom did you hand something to? If you pray, give thanks in words from your tradition for what continued.
Bat kol. An echo of a heavenly voice, still heard, the Talmud says, after the Tanakh closed and prophecy went quiet. Today's word.
Your line: the pages ran out; the handing-on didn't. Prophecy went quiet, and the teachers took up the chain. Day eight hundred eighty-seven, done.

888.title: Greeks arrive
888.hook: Alexander reaches the land, and Greek culture spreads
888.howItsDone: Jewish students learn the saying of Shimon the Righteous in Pirkei Avot, that the world stands on Torah, service and acts of loving-kindness, and the Talmud's legend of his meeting with Alexander is told in study of the Second Temple period.

segments.voice: Yesterday we stepped off the last page of the Tanakh, and a chain of teachers picked it up. Your line was the pages ran out; the handing-on didn't. Today, a king from Macedonia.

The first book of Maccabees opens at a gallop. Alexander, son of Philip, the Macedonian, comes out of the land the book calls Chettiim, defeats Darius, king of the Persians. He takes cities, kills kings, and goes to the ends of the earth, until, in the King James words, "the earth was quiet before him." Soon he falls sick, knows he is dying, and divides his kingdom among his servants. He reigned twelve years, the book says. A storm that passes. But what he left behind did not pass: Greek language, Greek cities, Greek ways of living arrive in the land of Israel and stay.
screen: `A KING FROM MACEDONIA.` → `THE EARTH WAS QUIET BEFORE HIM.` → `THE STORM PASSES. THE CULTURE STAYS.`

segments.voice: The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, tells the meeting as a legend. Alexander's army is marching toward Jerusalem. The high priest, Shimon the Righteous, puts on his priestly garments and, with the city's leaders carrying torches, walks all night to meet him. When Alexander sees him, the conqueror gets down from his chariot and bows. His men are shocked. Alexander explains: this is the face I see before me when I win my battles. The Temple is spared. Two worlds meet, and the surprise is who bows. Shimon the Righteous is the man Pirkei Avot names right after the Great Assembly, the one who said the world stands on three things: Torah, service, and acts of loving-kindness. So the legend puts the heir of the chain face to face with the man who conquered the world. But meeting isn't always bowing. In the first book of Maccabees, some in Israel say, let's make a covenant with the nations around us, and they build a place of exercise in Jerusalem after the customs of the nations. The book is not pleased. Two cultures meet, and the meeting goes in every direction: respect, borrowing, worry, conflict. The Hebrew name for Greece, Yavan, turns up in the book of Daniel too: the kingdom of Yavan comes after Persia. The question for the next few days: how do you live inside someone else's culture and stay yourself?
screen: `THE CONQUEROR BOWS.` · then, large: `TORAH, SERVICE, LOVING-KINDNESS.` · `A PLACE OF EXERCISE IN JERUSALEM.` · `INSIDE A CULTURE, STILL YOURSELF?`

segments.voice: Walk through an ordinary day in your mind, the gym, a class, a word you use, and find one thing you suspect came from Greek culture; if you're not sure, just hold the question. Then find one thing from your own family, people or tradition, and let both sit side by side without picking a winner. If you pray, use words from your tradition for the places you live.
Greeks arrive. Alexander sweeps through, and Greek language and ways of life settle into the land of Israel. Today's word.
Your line: two cultures meet. Sometimes the meeting is a bow, sometimes a quarrel. See you tomorrow.

889.title: The Torah in Greek
889.hook: the Torah is translated into Greek; legend says by seventy-two elders
889.carry: something always stays behind in the original
889.howItsDone: Jews today read the Torah in Hebrew in the synagogue and study it in many languages, often with a translation printed beside the Hebrew; the Talmud's story of the seventy-two elders is taught in tractate Megillah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alexander came through like a storm, and in the legend he bowed to the high priest. Your line was two cultures meet. Today, the Torah itself crosses into Greek.

A king sends for seventy-two elders. That's how the Talmud tells it, in tractate Megillah. King Ptolemy gathers them, and before they can talk to each other, he puts each one in a separate house. He doesn't tell them why. Then he goes to each man alone: write for me the Torah of Moses your teacher. In Greek. Seventy-two rooms, seventy-two pens, no way to compare notes. Anyone who has translated knows the problem: a sentence can have more than one right answer. So what comes out of those rooms?
screen: `SEVENTY-TWO ELDERS.` → `SEVENTY-TWO SEPARATE HOUSES.` → `WRITE FOR ME THE TORAH.`

segments.voice: The same thing, every time. The Talmud says God put wisdom in each one's heart, and all of them agreed. Each made the same small changes, where a word-for-word Greek version might be misread by a king. The very first line is one. Hebrew opens with in the beginning, then created, then God. Read too literally, a Greek reader might think in the beginning was the one doing the creating. So all seventy-two wrote God created in the beginning. In the legend, careful translation is a kind of guarding. And the rabbis had more than one feeling about it. In the Mishnah, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that besides Hebrew, the holy books may be written in Greek. The Talmud finds a reason in Noah's blessing, in the King James words: "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem." The rabbis read it as the beauty of Japheth, the Greek language, dwelling in the tents of Shem, Israel's house of study. But the minor tractate Soferim remembers a Greek translation made for King Ptolemy as a hard day, as hard for Israel as the day the golden calf was made, because the Torah could not be fully translated. A gift that lets the Torah travel. A loss, because something always stays behind in the original. Anyone reading a verse in English today stands inside that old argument.
screen: `ALL SEVENTY-TWO AGREE.` · `GOD CREATED IN THE BEGINNING.` · then, large: `GOD SHALL ENLARGE JAPHETH.` · `A GIFT, AND A HARD DAY.`

segments.voice: Take one verse, Noah's blessing from today if nothing else is at hand, and read it slowly. Which word might be carrying something it can't quite hold? If you know a little Hebrew, look at the Hebrew too; if you pray, give thanks for whoever carried this text into your language.
Megillah, the Talmud tractate that tells how seventy-two elders in separate rooms all wrote the same Greek translation of the Torah. Today's word.

Your line: something always stays behind in the original. That ends a week that began with three parts, one library, then a doubt didn't throw a book out, plain meaning first, where the verse breathes is where its thought divides, the pages ran out, the handing-on didn't, and two cultures meet. Day eight hundred eighty-nine.
